claims.text: Toughness retention or loss in high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and grain-boundary-mediated fracture.
The proposed material is a high-entropy alloy with a defined composition and microstructure.
Grain size is to be changed under controlled conditions.
Alloy composition is an alternative controlled intervention.
The hypothesis applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
Dislocation density mediates the effect of the intervention on toughness.
Grain-boundary character mediates the effect of the intervention on toughness.
Dislocation glide is a mechanism governing toughness.
Grain-boundary sliding is a mechanism governing toughness.
Increasing grain size will improve toughness relative to the as-cast alloy.
Optimizing alloy composition will improve toughness relative to the as-cast alloy.
The toughness of the as-cast alloy serves as the baseline.
The hypothesis is intended to hold for grain sizes from 1 to 100 micrometres.
The hypothesis is intended to hold only for compositions within a single-phase solid-solution region.
Precipitates or defects may influence toughness independently of the proposed governing variables.
A systematic grain-size or composition series can test the hypothesis using quasi-static tensile testing and microstructural characterization.
Absence of a correlation between toughness and grain size or alloy composition would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The governing competition is framed as dislocation-mediated plasticity versus grain-boundary-mediated fracture, but the stated mechanism substitutes grain-boundary sliding for grain-boundary fracture. Sliding and fracture are not equivalent, and their relationship is not explained.
